title: Tukaram and the bhajan
hookLine: devotional songs in everyday words, and the poet whose notebooks came back

cards: Almost four hundred years ago, beside the Indrayani river in Maharashtra, a shopkeeper named Tukaram was writing songs to God.
Not in Sanskrit, the language of priests and scholars, but in Marathi, the language his neighbors spoke at the market. People sang them everywhere.
Some learned men were furious: who was this shopkeeper, from a caste that wasn't supposed to teach scripture, to put sacred truths in street language?
So, the story goes, Tukaram was told to sink his notebooks in the river. He did. Then he sat down on the bank and prayed, without eating, for thirteen days.

teach.b: On the thirteenth day, the tradition says, the notebooks rose to the surface, unharmed, and came back to him. Many tell it as a miracle.
Some read it another way: the people carried the songs back, because they already knew them by heart. Either way, the songs lived.
Tukaram's songs, called abhangas, are still sung by the warkaris, pilgrims who walk to the temple of Vitthala at Pandharpur every year, singing the whole way.
That's the teaching in this story, and it's one of Hinduism's biggest: bhakti, devotion, belongs to everyone. Not only to people who know Sanskrit, or were born into the right family.
The word bhajan comes from the same root as bhakti, your sixteenth word: bhaj, to share in, to adore.
A bhajan is bhakti you can sing. Bhajans are simple: short lines, lots of repetition, in the languages people actually speak, Hindi, Marathi, Gujarati, Bengali, Tamil and many more.
Mirabai, the princess you met on day sixteen, sang hers for Krishna. One that many people know, sung at Gandhi's prayer meetings, begins: Raghupati raghava raja ram, patita pavana sita ram.
Lord of the line of Raghu, King Ram; purifier of the fallen, Sita and Ram.
And bhajans are usually sung together: a temple hall, or a living room with the sofas pushed back, a harmonium, a drum, tiny cymbals going ching, ching, and half the room off-key. Nobody's checking.
The tradition doesn't ask for a pretty voice, or perfect Hindi. It asks for a whole one.

how: Many Hindus gather in homes and temples, often weekly, to sing bhajans, simple devotional songs in regional languages, many by medieval poet-saints such as Tukaram and Mirabai, with harmonium, drums and small cymbals; Marathi warkari pilgrims sing Tukaram's abhangas on the walk to Pandharpur.

games.q: you're Tukaram. learned men say a shopkeeper has no right to sing about God in marathi, and tell you to sink your songs in the river. what do you do?
o: argue with them until they give up.
sink them, then sit by the river and pray.
games.why: he sank them and prayed on the bank for thirteen days, and the story says they came back up. bhakti belongs to every voice.

practice: Sing the line, or sing it inside if you're somewhere you can't: Raghupati raghava raja ram, patita pavana sita ram. Once slowly, then a little louder than feels comfortable, without worrying about the tune or the pronunciation.
If you'd rather, sing any song of devotion you know, in whatever language you actually speak. Then stop, and sit in the ringing quiet afterward.

wordCard.voice: Bhajan. A devotional song, simple and repeated, in everyday language, usually sung together: bhakti you can sing. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit/Hindi bhajana: adoration; a devotional song. From the root bhaj, as in bhakti.
